citation: Caine, N. (1980). The rainfall intensity-duration control of shallow landslides and debris flows. Geografiska Annaler A, 62, 23-27.
region: Global
data_size: Not verifiable from accessible source; no count inferred.
method: Original global rainfall intensity-duration threshold study; exact equation omitted because full text inaccessible.
validation_design: Not verifiable.
key_metric: Not reported.
caveat: Global heterogeneous prior; not Rwanda-calibrated.
relevance: Historical ID prior only.
quality_rating: Moderate bibliographic evidence; low quantitative usability.
source_type: Peer-reviewed; DOI landing page read, full text inaccessible

citation: Guzzetti, F., Peruccacci, S., Rossi, M., & Stark, C. P. (2008). The rainfall intensity-duration control of shallow landslides and debris flows: an update. Landslides, 5, 3-17.
region: Global literature/database
data_size: 2,626 rainfall events causing shallow landslides or debris flows.
method: Objective log-log ID threshold; rainfall normalized by mean annual precipitation and rainy-day normal; durations 10 min to 35 days.
validation_design: No independent local/geographic validation reported in accessible text.
key_metric: Scope and database size verified; no predictive score reported.
caveat: Literature/reporting selection and heterogeneous processes; normalization cannot remove local Rwanda bias.
relevance: Weak global prior for sensitivity analysis.
quality_rating: High for stated scope and sample; coefficients not reproduced.

citation: Brunetti, M. T., et al. (2010). Rainfall thresholds for the possible occurrence of landslides in Italy. NHESS, 10, 447-458.
region: Italy; national and Abruzzo analyses
data_size: 753 rainfall events resulting in landslides.
method: Bayesian and frequentist threshold methods; multiple exceedance-probability ID thresholds and four-level warning scheme.
validation_design: No independent prospective validation or numeric skill score verified.
key_metric: Source states Bayesian more suited to small datasets and frequentist better for large datasets.
caveat: Heterogeneous catalogue and process mix; small subsets can be unstable.
relevance: Supports Bayesian/uncertainty-first treatment for small local samples.
quality_rating: High.
source_type: Peer-reviewed open access; full abstract read

citation: Berti, M., et al. (2012). Probabilistic rainfall thresholds for landslide occurrence using a Bayesian approach. JGR Earth Surface, 117, F04006.
region: Emilia-Romagna, Italy; about 12,000 km2
data_size: 4,141 historical landslides; 2,741 well-defined events; 1,573 duplicates removed, leaving 1,168 distinct triggers; 176 gauges; 250,177 non-triggering rainfall events.
method: Bayesian probability conditional on event intensity-duration and other rainfall variables; automated event detection calibrated at 3-day/5-mm settings.
validation_design: No random split; sensitivity analysis varied uncertain events, event definitions, detector settings and catalogue period.
key_metric: A 2-day, 40-mm/day event probability was 0.15 within about 65 km2 and 0.80 within about 2,600 km2; event-detection RMSEP used.
caveat: Daily rainfall; mixed landslide types/materials; 24% undefined and 10% uncertain trigger events; probability depends on reference area.
relevance: Template for probabilistic, area-specific inference with explicit event uncertainty.
quality_rating: High.

citation: Peruccacci, S., et al. (2012). Lithological and seasonal control on rainfall thresholds for the possible initiation of landslides in central Italy. Geomorphology, 139-140, 79-90.
region: Abruzzo, Marche and Umbria, central Italy
data_size: 442 rainfall events with landslides, February 2002-August 2010; subsets by region, lithology and season.
method: Frequentist ED thresholds linking cumulative event rainfall and duration; bootstrap parameter uncertainty.
validation_design: No independent holdout verified.
key_metric: Bootstrap uncertainty; no external predictive score reported in accessible text.
caveat: 8.5-year record; stratification reduces n and can confound physical with catalogue effects.
relevance: Shows ED/uncertainty analysis is feasible with hundreds, but stability with 88 is doubtful.
quality_rating: High.

citation: Melillo, M., et al. (2016). Rainfall thresholds for the possible landslide occurrence in Sicily based on automatic reconstruction. Landslides, 13, 165-172.
region: Sicily, Italy
data_size: 229 landslides (2002-2012); 169 gauges; 29,270 reconstructed rainfall events; 472 possible trigger ED conditions.
method: Automated reproducible reconstruction of rainfall events, multiple ED conditions and empirical thresholds.
validation_design: No independent temporal/prospective validation reported in accessible text.
key_metric: Reconstructed event/condition counts verified; no predictive score reported.
caveat: 472 conditions exceed 229 landslides because multiple conditions are reconstructed; depends on preset parameters and event timing.
relevance: Supports reproducible event reconstruction before fitting sparse-data thresholds.
quality_rating: High.

citation: Gariano, S. L., et al. (2015). Calibration and validation of rainfall thresholds for shallow landslide forecasting in Sicily. Geomorphology, 228, 653-665.
region: Sicily, Italy
data_size: Calibration: 200 rainfall conditions/223 landslides, 2002-2011. Validation: 29 landslide rainfall events in 2012.
method: Frequentist ED thresholds with exceedance probabilities; contingency tables, skill scores and ROC.
validation_design: True later-year back-analysis (2012 holdout) after 2002-2011 calibration.
key_metric: Contingency/skill/ROC metrics used; numeric values omitted because not fully exposed in accessible text.
caveat: Large-area missing landslides make true negatives and false positives uncertain.
relevance: Model validation pattern for Rwanda: use a later-year holdout, not random in-sample evaluation.
quality_rating: High; numeric performance intentionally omitted.

citation: Rossi, M., et al. (2017). Statistical approaches for the definition of landslide rainfall thresholds and their uncertainty using rain gauge and satellite data. Geomorphology, 285, 16-27.
region: Umbria, central Italy; about 8,456 km2
data_size: 187 rainfall-induced landslides, 2002-2010; 60 gauges plus TMPA satellite estimates.
method: Expert and automated event reconstruction; ED thresholds from gauge/satellite data using three statistical approaches and rainfall-data uncertainty.
validation_design: Validation performances compared across data products/methods; exact scores omitted.
key_metric: Paper reports a prior Peruccacci result that about 175 events were needed to keep threshold uncertainty below 10% in that setting; this is not a universal power calculation.
caveat: Only 187 events; rainfall, timing and inventory errors affect uncertainty and apparent skill.
relevance: Closest evidence for a minimum-sample warning: 88 is below the cited context-specific benchmark.
quality_rating: High; qualification retained.

citation: Monsieurs, E., et al. (2019). A susceptibility-based rainfall threshold approach for landslide occurrence in the western branch of the East African Rift. NHESS, 19, 775-797.
region: Western East African Rift; about 350,000 km2
data_size: 174 events, 2001-2018; 29 mining events discarded; 143 non-mining calibration points after additional exclusions.
method: Susceptibility-based frequentist threshold using TMPA-RT/TRMM rainfall aggregated to daily; bootstrap lower-envelope regression.
validation_design: No independent temporal holdout verified; same-period pixel example.
key_metric: In an example pixel with six events, 5% and 10% thresholds had zero observed false negatives but 4,715 and 4,242 above-threshold days (about 70% and 63% of the series). Illustrative, not regional skill.
caveat: Incomplete and spatially biased media inventory; uncertain dates/processes; TMPA-RT average underestimation about 40%; warning area is coarse.
relevance: Closest East African analogue and direct warning against transferring global thresholds or ignoring missed events.
quality_rating: High.
source_type: Peer-reviewed open access; full text read

citation: Uwihirwe, J., Hrachowitz, M., & Bogaard, T.A. (2020). Landslide precipitation thresholds in Rwanda. Landslides, 17, 2469–2481.
region: Rwanda, Central-East Africa; emphasis includes the northwestern Mukungwa catchment
data_size: Rainfall from 35 gauges over 2006–2018; 22 gauges were selected as representative for landslide conditions. The accessible article text does not state a single verified event count; it states that the inventory is dominated by hazardous/fatal or highly damaging reports and likely misses nonhazardous events.
method: Empirical-statistical trigger and trigger-cause threshold analysis. Same-day/event rainfall variables were paired with antecedent precipitation indices (API5, API10, API30) using decay coefficient k=0.95 as a proxy for accumulated soil moisture. Rainfall data were daily and gauge-based.
validation_design: ROC/AUC assessed explanatory/discriminatory power; Bayesian probabilities, maximum true-skill statistic and minimum radial distance selected thresholds. The accessible source does not document an independent holdout or provide a verified external-test design.
key_metric: Event precipitation volume, same-day cumulative 1-day rainfall (RD1) and 10-day antecedent precipitation were the most discriminative variables. Single trigger thresholds had the most true-positive alarms but a high false-positive rate; combining trigger and antecedent variables in bilinear form improved prediction. Numerical AUC values are omitted because they were not verified in the accessible text.
caveat: Gauge-based point observations, sparse network and uncertain event locations; reported-landslide ascertainment favors severe events, producing selection bias; thresholds are regional empirical associations and do not isolate rainfall from geology, land use or drainage. High false positives remain for single-variable triggers.
relevance: Directly supports testing several antecedent windows rather than one arbitrary lag and warns that same-day rainfall alone can generate excessive false alarms in Rwanda. API is a proxy, not measured soil moisture.
quality_rating: High for Rwanda threshold evidence; moderate for exact event-count and out-of-sample claims because those details were not verifiable in the accessible text.
source_type: Peer-reviewed research article; authoritative DOI/full-text landing page read

citation: Riveros, A., Wanjala, H., Schellekens, J., Sperna Weiland, F., Hrachowitz, M., & Bogaard, T.A. (2022). Potential of satellite-derived hydro-meteorological information for landslide initiation thresholds in Rwanda. Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences, 22, 3641–3661.
region: Rwanda; mountainous central-eastern Africa, including Kivu, upper Nyabarongo and Mukungwa catchments
data_size: 55 accurately dated landslides in 2007–2019; 32 in modeled catchments; 19 Rwanda Meteorology Agency gauges; 6 AWS soil-moisture stations. Inventory location accuracy was typically 5–25 km and a 5-km buffer was used.
method: Compared seven daily satellite/reanalysis precipitation products to weighted representative gauges using RMSE, Pearson correlation and relative bias; evaluated satellite near-surface soil moisture (top 5 cm) and Wflow model soil moisture at 50 cm and 2 m against AWS observations; constructed single-variable and bilinear rainfall–antecedent-moisture thresholds. IMERG, CHIRPS, TRMM 3B42, ERA5 and other products were tested; Wflow was driven by ERA5 meteorology.
validation_design: Gauge/product comparisons used the 19-gauge benchmark; threshold discrimination used ROC/AUC and operating-point metrics (TPR/FPR, TSS and minimum radial distance). No independent temporal or spatial holdout is reported in the verified article text; the landslide inventory is event-selected and sparse.
key_metric: IMERG was consistently the most suitable product by RMSE/CC/RB; ERA5 was least suitable in the comparison. For 30-day cumulative rainfall scatterplots, CHIRPS R=0.67 and IMERG R=0.60. Three-day rainfall had AUC approximately 0.72 and TPR approximately 80%; 50-cm modeled root-zone moisture had AUC approximately 0.74 and TPR 84%. Bilinear moisture–rainfall models reduced false alarms by approximately 20% with an approximately 8% reduction in true alarms.
caveat: Only 55 accurately dated events, with likely under-reporting of nonfatal/non-damaging landslides; spatial mismatch between point gauges, 5-km buffers and gridded products; soil-moisture depths differ (5 cm, 50 cm, 2 m versus AWS 20 cm); no verified independent holdout. Results are threshold-model evidence, not proof of ML generalization.
relevance: Closest direct evidence for a Rwanda EWS: supports using antecedent moisture as a state variable with multi-day rainfall triggers and shows that product choice matters. It is also the strongest verified evidence that IMERG may be preferable to CHIRPS/ERA5 for this specific Rwanda sample, but it does not validate ERA5-Land in Rwanda.
quality_rating: High for Rwanda relevance and source accessibility; moderate for operational generalization because the inventory is biased and validation is not clearly out-of-sample.

citation: Ahmed, J.S., Buizza, R., Dell’Acqua, M., Demissie, T., & Pè, M.E. (2024). Evaluation of ERA5 and CHIRPS rainfall estimates against observations across Ethiopia. Meteorology and Atmospheric Physics, 136, 17.
region: Ethiopia, including North-Central, Northwestern and East-Central highlands and lowlands; complex topography and diverse climates
data_size: 167 independent high-quality NMA rain gauges; daily data from 1981–2018. Stations contributing to CHIRPS/ERA5 development were excluded from evaluation.
method: Point-to-pixel comparison at common 0.25° resolution for daily, monthly, seasonal and annual rainfall. Metrics were modified KGE, RMSE, PBIAS, probability of detection, false-alarm ratio and frequency bias; six homogeneous rainfall clusters were formed with k-means.
validation_design: Independent gauge set relative to product development stations; point-to-pixel evaluation over the full 1981–2018 period. No ML train/test split is applicable or reported; this is product validation.
key_metric: At daily scale, CHIRPS KGE was predominantly 0.3–0.6 in high-altitude areas above 2000 m; ERA5 performed poorly around 2000–3500 m. CHIRPS generally outperformed ERA5 in highlands and complex terrain. For violent rainfall above 40 mm/day, FAR exceeded 0.7 for both products; both overestimated light-event frequency and ERA5 generally underestimated heavy/violent-event frequency.
caveat: Ethiopia is a transfer region, not Rwanda; CHIRPS was evaluated at 0.25° rather than its finer native option; point-to-pixel mismatch remains; lowland skill was poor and attributed partly to sparse gauge density. Results concern ERA5, not ERA5-Land.
relevance: Strong East African highland comparison showing that product skill is elevation- and intensity-dependent, supporting region/season-stratified calibration and caution against assuming ERA5 or CHIRPS is uniformly reliable for landslide-trigger rainfall.
quality_rating: High for independent gauge validation and mountainous East African transfer; moderate for Rwanda applicability and ERA5-Land inference.
source_type: Peer-reviewed research article; author/institutional full-text PDF read

citation: Dinku, T., Funk, C., Peterson, P., Maidment, R., Tadesse, T., Gadain, H., & Ceccato, P. (2018). Validation of the CHIRPS satellite rainfall estimates over eastern Africa. Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society, 144, 292–312.
region: Eastern Africa, including mountainous and coastal regions
data_size: Approximately 1,200 rain-gauge stations; daily, dekadal (10-day) and monthly evaluations.
method: Compared CHIRP and gauge-merged CHIRPS against gauge data and against ARC2 and TAMSAT operational satellite rainfall products at multiple temporal scales.
validation_design: Gauge comparison at daily, dekadal and monthly scales; no ML holdout. The USGS record reports spatially variable performance and does not provide a Rwanda-specific independent result.
key_metric: CHIRP/CHIRPS were significantly better than ARC2, with higher skill and low or no bias; they were slightly better than TAMSAT at dekadal/monthly scales, while TAMSAT performed better at daily scale. Performance was weak in coastal and mountainous regions. No unsupported numerical scores are added.
caveat: Gauge network is uneven; product gauge merging can create dependence between reference and product; weak mountain performance is directly relevant but not Rwanda-specific; daily extremes may be less reliable than longer accumulations.
relevance: Foundational East African evidence that CHIRPS skill is not spatially uniform and that daily landslide-trigger applications can differ from 10-day antecedent/climatological applications.
quality_rating: High for regional product-comparison evidence; moderate for direct Rwanda transfer.
source_type: Peer-reviewed research article; USGS authoritative publication record read

citation: Dezfuli, A.K., Ichoku, C.M., Huffman, G.J., Mohr, K.I., Selker, J.S., van de Giesen, N., Hochreutener, R., & Annor, F.O. (2017). Validation of IMERG precipitation in Africa. Journal of Hydrometeorology, 18, 2817–2825.
region: Tropical Africa; East African point site Lela Primary School, Kenya, plus Kumasi and Navrongo, Ghana; continent-wide IMERG/TMPA comparison
data_size: Three quality-controlled TAHMO stations with most of rainy-season 2015 data for daily evaluation; three additional stations only for diurnal analysis. East African Lela Primary School had February–December 2015 coverage.
method: Validated half-hourly IMERG-V04A against high-frequency gauges; compared annual/diurnal cycles and daily distributions with TMPA, GPCC and CHIRPS. Used CC, MAD, multiplicative bias, POD, FAR, frequency bias, CSI and HSS.
validation_design: Point comparisons at the three stations and spatial IMERG-versus-TMPA diagnostics across Africa. IMERG Final Run was GPCC-gauge calibrated, so this is not fully independent gauge validation; only one year is available.
key_metric: At Lela Primary School, IMERG had CC 0.54, MAD 0.81, multiplicative bias 1.04, POD 0.84, FAR 0.17, frequency bias 1.02, CSI 0.71 and HSS 0.58. CHIRPS showed the largest gauge differences at that site, especially during short rains and extreme daily rates. IMERG captured the diurnal cycle better than TMPA, but clear overall superiority was not established.
caveat: Very small station sample and one-year record; point-versus-grid mismatch; IMERG Final Run uses GPCC gauge calibration; Kenyan site is not Rwanda and is not a mountainous Rwanda gauge; CHIRPS comparison is ancillary rather than a full product intercomparison.
relevance: Useful negative/cautionary evidence: higher temporal resolution does not guarantee uniformly better daily or extreme-event skill, and product rankings vary by site and season.
quality_rating: High for documented methods/metrics; low-to-moderate for Rwanda generalization due to sparse, short, non-Rwanda sample.

citation: Omay, P.O., Muthama, N.J., Oludhe, C., Kinama, J.M., Artan, G., & Atheru, Z. (2025). Evaluation of satellite-based rainfall estimates over the IGAD region of Eastern Africa. Meteorology and Atmospheric Physics, 137, 22.
region: IGAD region of Eastern Africa, with five subregions and varied mountains, highlands, deserts and semi-arid zones
data_size: 105 rain-gauge observations; nine satellite rainfall products; 2001–2020; seasonal evaluations for MAM, JJAS and OND.
method: Gauge/product comparison using rainfall totals, annual cycle, 24 continuous metrics, categorical and volumetric metrics, scatterplots, CDFs and spatial portraits, evaluated at each gauge and by subregion.
validation_design: Multi-metric point validation at the 105 gauges; no ML holdout reported. Authors explicitly caution that a single metric is insufficient, especially in complex topography.
key_metric: CMORPH-RT ranked best overall, followed by CHIRPS v2; CHIRPS, CPC-RFEv2 and GPM-IMERG were among the top four. Products slightly underestimated rainfall overall; skill was better over highlands than desert/semi-arid regions and lower in JJAS than MAM/OND.
caveat: The abstract does not provide product-specific numerical scores; station density/distribution strongly affects validation; IGAD-scale averages may conceal Rwanda subregional behavior; ERA5-Land is not one of the reported products in the verified abstract.
relevance: Recent regional evidence for using multiple products/metrics and for stratifying calibration by terrain and season; supports ensemble or uncertainty-aware features rather than one-product dependence.
quality_rating: High for regional comparative conclusions; moderate for Rwanda-specific inference because exact Rwanda subset scores were not verified.
source_type: Peer-reviewed research article; authoritative DOI/agency publication page read

citation: Abraham, M.T., Satyam, N., Reddy, S.K.P., Pradhan, B., Rosi, A., et al. (2021). Usage of antecedent soil moisture for improving the performance of rainfall thresholds for landslide early warning. Catena, 200, 105147.
region: Idukki district, Kerala, southern India; humid monsoon Western Ghats
data_size: 225 landslide events were considered; CTRL-T retained 177 events and discarded the remainder because responsible rainfall conditions could not be identified, including spatial/temporal uncertainty related to gauge distance and delay.
method: Compared empirical rainfall event-duration thresholds and Bayesian probabilistic thresholds using rainfall severity plus averaged passive-microwave soil-moisture estimates. ROC curves were used to compare models.
validation_design: ROC/AUC model comparison; no independent temporal/spatial holdout is stated in the accessible record and full text was not publicly accessible in this run.
key_metric: The rainfall-plus-soil-wetness probabilistic threshold had AUC 0.96 and was reported as more sensitive/specific than conventional rainfall-only approaches. Lower antecedent moisture required more severe rainfall; wet soil allowed less severe rainfall to trigger landslides.
caveat: Non-East-African transfer study; 48 events were discarded; publisher full text was inaccessible, so exact product/version, split design and additional confusion-matrix metrics are not reported here. AUC may reflect in-sample threshold comparison rather than prospective performance.
relevance: Mechanistic and statistical support for conditioning rainfall intensity/duration on antecedent wetness, but the high AUC should not be transplanted to Rwanda or interpreted as ML generalization.
quality_rating: Moderate: authoritative abstract/record and DOI verified, but full article access was restricted and external validation is not verified.
source_type: Peer-reviewed research article; authoritative DOI landing page and institutional record read; publisher full text was access-restricted

citation: Gonzalez, F.C.G., Cavacanti, M.C.R., Ribeiro, W.N., Mendonça, M.B., & Haddad, A.N. (2023/2024). A systematic review on rainfall thresholds for landslides occurrence. Heliyon, 10(1), e23247.
region: Global literature review; not Rwanda-specific
data_size: 225 rainfall-threshold papers from 2008–2021; 178 used statistical or hybrid methods. Among statistical-threshold papers that included additional factors, 15 used soil-water variables (reported as 59.3% of that subset).
method: Systematic review and classification of rainfall-threshold methods, accumulated/antecedent periods and additional hydrological variables such as soil water, pore pressure, water table and subsurface flow.
validation_design: No new predictive validation dataset; evidence synthesis. The review notes that 118/178 statistical papers used only one rainfall observation period and 53 used two, with timing/overlap differing.
key_metric: No pooled predictive metric. The review reports that preceding rainfall increases soil moisture and changes the additional rainfall needed for failure; in humid regions with rainfall distributed through the year, preceding rainfall may have less influence. It notes no evidence in its summarized patterns that low-intensity short-duration rain alone triggers landslides.
caveat: Heterogeneous definitions, climates, landslide types, inventories and threshold periods; not a Rwanda validation; review-level counts do not imply causal effect sizes. One rainfall window can confound preparatory and triggering rain, and tropical/wet-season processes may require minute/hourly resolution.
relevance: Supports testing multiple antecedent windows and soil-state variables, while warning against a one-size-fits-all API and against interpreting review prevalence as evidence of operational benefit.
quality_rating: High for broad synthesis and caveats; low for Rwanda-specific numerical transfer.

citation: Xie, W., et al. (2022). The evaluation of IMERG and ERA5-Land daily precipitation over China with considering the influence of gauge data bias. Scientific Reports, 12.
region: China, including plains, plateaus and mountainous areas; not East Africa
data_size: Daily IMERG and ERA5-Land with gauge precipitation over 2005–2016; the accessible article does not expose a verified gauge count in the returned text and gauge data were proprietary/confidential.
method: Compared IMERG and ERA5-Land against original versus bias-corrected gauge data, correcting wind undercatch, wetting loss and trace error. Metrics included relative bias, Kling–Gupta efficiency, frequency bias and critical success index across locations, seasons, climate zones, intensity classes and precipitation phase.
validation_design: Benchmark sensitivity analysis, not an independent holdout; conclusions explicitly depend on whether raw or corrected gauges are used.
key_metric: After gauge-bias correction, relative biases of both IMERG and ERA5-Land declined; frequency bias and detection changed by event class, season, location and precipitation phase. The paper does not establish a universal winner for Rwanda-like terrain.
caveat: China-only transfer; gauge correction has uncertainty and gauge exposure/hourly wind metadata were unavailable; proprietary gauges prevent independent reproduction; not an East African mountain validation.
relevance: The key ERA5-Land caution for Rwanda: apparent product skill can be an artifact of biased gauge benchmarks, so calibration/evaluation should quantify gauge uncertainty and avoid treating one gridded product as truth. No verified Rwanda ERA5-Land head-to-head study was found.
quality_rating: High for gauge-benchmark uncertainty and ERA5-Land methodology; low for geographic transfer to Rwanda.
source_type: Peer-reviewed open-access research article; PMC full text read

citation: Brenning, A. (2005). Spatial prediction models for landslide hazards: review, comparison and evaluation. Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences, 5, 853–862.
region: Ecuadorian Andes case study
data_size: Not stated in the accessible article abstract; detailed count not verified
method: Logistic regression with stepwise backward selection; support-vector machines; bootstrap-aggregated classification trees (bagging/double-bagging)
validation_design: Resampling that accounts for spatial autocorrelation; independent test sets; estimates for present/future landslides within and outside the training area
key_metric: Misclassification error rates; no numeric values were reported in the accessible abstract
caveat: Detailed inventory composition and numerical results were not accessible through the article abstract extraction; do not use this record for an exact sample-size claim
relevance: Direct negative evidence against assuming complex tree models generalize: logistic regression had the lowest error and best generalization, while tree methods tended to overfit outside the training area
quality_rating: Peer-reviewed and directly read at the journal landing page; abstract-level access for quantitative details

citation: Goetz, J.N., Brenning, A., Petschko, H., & Leopold, P. (2015). Evaluating machine learning and statistical prediction techniques for landslide susceptibility modeling. Computers & Geosciences, 81, 1–11.
region: Three 50-km² areas in Lower Austria, Austria, with different geological/morphological settings
data_size: Not stated in the accessible article extraction; exact landslide/inventory count not verified
method: Logistic regression (GLM), generalized additive model (GAM), weights of evidence (WoE), support-vector machine, random forest, and bootstrap-aggregated penalized discriminant analysis (BPLDA)
validation_design: Spatial k-fold cross-validation; predictor importance and map appearance also assessed
key_metric: AUROC and true-positive rate at 10% false-positive rate. Across AOIs, median AUROC differences ranged 2.9–8.9 percentage points and median TPR differences 11–15 percentage points; most performance differences were not statistically significant
caveat: No exact inventory count was available in the accessible extraction; three Austrian AOIs are not Rwanda and are not a small-n=88 experiment
relevance: Strongly relevant method-comparison evidence: no universal best model; apparent RF/BPLDA advantage was usually small/non-significant, while RF/BPLDA/WoE produced heterogeneous spatial artifacts and GLM/GAM/SVM smoother maps
quality_rating: Peer-reviewed article; actual ScienceDirect abstract/full-text sections read; sample-count detail not accessible

citation: Nsengiyumva, J.B., Luo, G., Amanambu, A.C., et al. (2019). Comparing probabilistic and statistical methods in landslide susceptibility modeling in Rwanda/Centre-Eastern Africa. Science of the Total Environment.
region: Entire Rwanda
data_size: 692 past landslide points; the accessible source states they were used to calibrate and validate, but does not expose a verified train/test partition
method: Weights of evidence, frequency ratio, logistic regression, and statistical index; 14 conditioning-factor maps
validation_design: ROC/AUC validation; exact split or spatial blocking was not stated in the accessible abstract/full-text extraction
key_metric: Prediction/AUC rates: WoE 92.7%, FR 86.9%, LR 81.2%, SI 79.5%
caveat: Inventory points and conditioning factors may be spatially biased; validation design is not clearly independent or spatially blocked in the accessible text; AUC alone does not establish calibration or transferability
relevance: Direct Rwanda evidence that simple FR/WoE/LR baselines are feasible and that method rankings can differ substantially, but the high AUCs should not be treated as unbiased regional generalization evidence
quality_rating: Peer-reviewed article; PubMed abstract and ScienceDirect article sections read

citation: Mind’je, R., Li, L., Nsengiyumva, J.B., Mupenzi, C., et al. (2020). Landslide susceptibility and influencing factors analysis in Rwanda. Environment, Development and Sustainability.
region: Rwanda
data_size: 423 landslide locations; 318 (75%) training and 105 (25%) validation, randomly split
method: Frequency-ratio model with GIS/remote sensing; ten influencing factors; multicollinearity checked using tolerance and VIF
validation_design: Random 75/25 point split; AUC success and prediction rates
key_metric: AUC 81.2% success rate and 84.6% prediction rate
caveat: Random point splitting can put spatially near or clustered observations in both sets; the study does not establish blocked spatial or temporal generalization; inventory completeness and representativeness remain concerns
relevance: A Rwanda FR benchmark and a cautionary example: a relatively small inventory can yield high AUC under random validation, so an 88-record biased inventory should not rely on this design
quality_rating: Peer-reviewed article; authoritative Springer landing page/abstract read

citation: Kumar, C., Walton, G., Santi, P., & Luza, C. (2025). Random cross-validation produces biased assessment of machine learning performance in regional landslide susceptibility prediction. Remote Sensing, 17(2), 213.
region: Arequipa Region, southern Peru (16,955 km²)
data_size: 1,460 mapped landslides; 24 landslide-influencing factors; non-landslide locations were also prepared, but the accessible text does not give a single final binary sample count
method: Logistic regression, LDA, KNN, ANN, SVM, RF, and C5.0; grid-search tuning
validation_design: Compared 10-fold random CV and 10-fold spatial CV (k-means clustering of coordinates), each with five repetitions; learning curves varied predictors (5–24) and training quantity (10–100%)
key_metric: Primary AUC, plus overall accuracy and recall. Random-CV estimates were 6–18% higher than spatial-CV estimates; example AUC changes with training quantity: KNN 0.83→0.90 random versus 0.80→0.83 spatial, and C5.0 0.86→0.92 random versus 0.82→0.86 spatial
caveat: Single regional Peru case, 1,460 mapped landslides rather than n≈88, and spatial CV is a design choice rather than a guarantee of temporal/event independence
relevance: Most direct current evidence for the proposed skeptical study: random CV overstated performance, falsely suggested gains from more variables, and the discrepancy was more noticeable for complex SVM/RF/C5.0 than simple LR/LDA; small spatially diverse data could outperform larger concentrated data
quality_rating: Peer-reviewed article; full MDPI article sections including methods/results/conclusions read

citation: Samodra, G., Ngadisih, & Nugroho, F.S. (2024). Benchmarking data handling strategies for landslide susceptibility modeling using random forest workflows.
region: Pacitan Regency, Indonesia, after Tropical Cyclone Cempaka (2017)
data_size: Complete inventory of 743 landslides; 11 controlling factors
method: Random forest under eight polygon-to-point inventory handling schemes: toe, scarp, center, one/random 3/5/10 points, and 15-m grid sampling; 24 workflows combined handling, CV, and tuning
validation_design: Compared non-spatial CV/non-spatial tuning, spatial CV/spatial tuning, and spatial CV with forward feature selection; exact fold count and numeric metric table were not available in the accessible abstract
key_metric: Abstract reports that 15-m grid sampling with spatial CV and spatial hyperparameter tuning minimized overfitting and produced relatively high predictive performance; no numeric AUC was verified
caveat: Single event and single Indonesian region; random-forest-only; abstract-level access means no unverified numeric metric is reported
relevance: Shows that apparent model behavior depends strongly on how a polygon inventory is converted to points and on spatial CV/tuning; directly relevant to biased, sparse inventories where pseudo-replication can inflate n
quality_rating: Peer-reviewed article; actual ScienceDirect abstract read; detailed full text/metrics inaccessible

citation: Alvioli, M., Loche, M., Jacobs, L., et al. (2024). A benchmark dataset and workflow for landslide susceptibility zonation. Earth-Science Reviews. DOI: 10.1016/j.earscirev.2024.104927.
region: Central Italy
data_size: 7,360 slope units covering about 4,100 km²
method: Benchmark workflow comparing independent statistical/machine-learning susceptibility implementations; final workflow constrained training, validation, and data use
validation_design: Benchmark-style constrained cross-validation/training workflow; exact fold design not stated in the accessible USGS record
key_metric: AUC values were rather similar after workflow constraints; Brier scores varied more and reflected predictive-ability differences
caveat: Not a small-inventory test and not Rwanda; the accessible agency record does not expose all model-specific implementation details
relevance: Agency-hosted benchmark evidence that implementation, training/validation choices, and probabilistic scoring can dominate apparent differences; supports reporting Brier/calibration-type metrics rather than AUC alone
quality_rating: Peer-reviewed Earth-Science Reviews paper verified through the USGS Publications Warehouse record; detailed full text not accessed
source_type: Peer-reviewed review/benchmark article; USGS-hosted authoritative record

citation: Nsengiyumva, J.B.; et al. (2018). Landslide Susceptibility Assessment Using Spatial Multi-Criteria Evaluation in Rwanda. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 15(2):243.
region: All Rwanda; national 1:1,000,000 map
data_size: 980 past landslide locations from documents, government/disaster databases, photos, GPS and field surveys; not 88 records.
method: Expert-weighted Spatial Multi-Criteria Evaluation using land cover, lithology, soil texture/depth, precipitation, slope, altitude and distance to roads; selected because of data shortage and incomplete data.
validation_design: Overlay comparison of all 980 locations with susceptibility classes; no train/test or temporal holdout. Reported distribution: 49.5% very high, 28% high, 17.8% moderate and 4.7% low; none very low.
key_metric: Those are overlay percentages; no ROC-AUC, calibration, precision/recall or prospective EWS metric reported.
caveat: Not physically based; expert weighting and inventory completeness/selection bias limit causal inference. Authors recommend maintaining national inventories and future quantitative/physically based work.
relevance: Rwanda baseline showing that even 980 locations were validated descriptively, cautioning against treating 88 biased records as independent evidence of ML/EWS skill.
quality_rating: High for Rwanda context because full article was read; contextual comparator, not evidence for SHALSTAB/TRIGRS/PINN performance.
source_type: Peer-reviewed Rwanda case study; full open-access article read

citation: Phillips SJ, Dudik M, Elith J, et al. (2009). Sample selection bias and presence-only distribution models: implications for background and pseudo-absence data. Ecological Applications 19:181-197.
region: 226 species from diverse regions worldwide
data_size: 226 species; exact record count not stated in accessed abstract
method: Presence-only models comparing random background with target-group background matched to occurrence-record sampling bias; covers GLM/GAM, boosted regression trees and Maxent
validation_design: Comparative performance across 226 species; exact resampling design not stated in accessed abstract
key_metric: Target-group background improved average performance; background choice had an effect as large as model choice; no numeric metric verified in accessed text
caveat: Requires information about sampling bias or a target group sharing it; does not guarantee unbiased absolute occurrence estimates
relevance: Direct evidence that naive pseudo-absence/background sampling can create environmental bias; supports bias-matched background or explicit observation-process modeling for Rwanda
quality_rating: High for presence-only bias; indirect to landslides
source_type: Peer-reviewed article; journal landing page and full abstract read

citation: Warton DI, Renner IW, Ramp D. (2013). Model-Based Control of Observer Bias for the Analysis of Presence-Only Data in Ecology. PLoS ONE 8:e79168.
region: Blue Mountains near Sydney, Australia; 86,227 km2; Myrtaceae plants
data_size: Evaluation used a separate systematically collected presence/absence dataset for 62 endemic Myrtaceae species; exact per-species counts not reported in accessed excerpt
method: Poisson point-process models with LASSO; environmental and accessibility/observer-bias covariates; predictions conditioned on common bias; compared with pseudo-absence correction
validation_design: Separate presence/absence data with 5-fold cross-validation
key_metric: AUC; abstract reports significant improvement and usually better performance than pseudo-absence/inventory correction; no pooled numeric AUC verified
caveat: Needs measurable bias covariates and assumes additive environment and bias effects; absolute occurrence intercept is not identifiable without extra information; inventory pseudo-absences can confound occurrence with species richness
relevance: Template for modeling reporting/accessibility bias rather than fabricating landslide absences; random 5-fold CV should not replace spatial/event holdouts
quality_rating: High method relevance; non-landslide domain
source_type: Peer-reviewed open-access article; full text read

citation: Hanberry BB, He HS, Palik BJ. (2012). Pseudoabsence Generation Strategies for Species Distribution Models. PLoS ONE 7:e44486.
region: Laurentian Mixed Forest, Minnesota, USA; about 4.9 million ha
data_size: 3,994 FIA plots containing 94,644 trees; tree species with at least 150 records; about 310,000 soil polygons
method: Random Forest with 16 predictors and four pseudo-absence strategies: random, two-step low-prediction, surveyed non-detections, and two-step surveyed
validation_design: 67% of presence polygons and up to 67% or 2,500 pseudo-absence polygons for modeling; remainder reserved; reserved surveyed non-detections used for AUC
key_metric: All strategies mean AUC at least 0.87; reported comparison had 0.95 for one-step strategies versus 0.87 for two-step strategies; high-probability predicted area differed from mean 0.14 for random to about 0.51 for two-step
caveat: Surveyed non-detections are not guaranteed true absences; AUC masked large map differences; forest-species domain
relevance: Good evidence that apparently good discrimination can coexist with materially different maps; pseudo-absence sensitivity should be primary Rwanda analysis
quality_rating: High for pseudo-absence sensitivity; indirect domain
source_type: Peer-reviewed open-access article; full text read

citation: Li F, Wang J, et al. (2022). Positive-unlabeled learning in bioinformatics and computational biology. Briefings in Bioinformatics 23:bbab461.
region: No single geography; bioinformatics and biomedical applications
data_size: Review of 29 PU-learning applications; not a landslide dataset
method: Reviews learning from a small labeled-positive set and a large unlabeled mixture; covers reliable-negative selection and direct PU classifiers
validation_design: Reviewed studies use k-fold CV, independent tests, leave-one-out and random tests; k-fold is most common
key_metric: Discusses AUPR and enrichment/precision measures such as EPR when true negatives are unavailable; no pooled benchmark metric
caveat: Evidence is bioinformatics-focused; class prior and unlabeled composition matter; overly small unlabeled sets can overfit; review recommends CV to reduce overestimation
relevance: Supports PU only if Rwanda unlabeled cells remain genuinely unlabeled and the observation process is modeled; does not validate a PU algorithm for 88 records
quality_rating: High conceptual review; indirect domain
source_type: Peer-reviewed review; publisher page/full article text read

citation: Goetz JN, Brenning A. (2022). Transfer learning for landslide susceptibility modeling using domain adaptation and case-based reasoning. Geoscientific Model Development 15:8765-8786.
region: 10 study areas in Austria, southern Ecuador and northern Italy; 1, 10 and 25 m resolutions
data_size: For domain adaptation, 50,000 unlabeled target points and 30,000 labeled source points were randomly selected as reference sets; exact inventory counts vary by area
method: Generalized additive landslide-susceptibility models using case-based reasoning, domain adaptation and combined CBR-DA
validation_design: Each area served as an unseen target; target labels excluded from training; target-area test data; AUROC
key_metric: CBR and CBR-DA were comparable to target-trained benchmarks; CBR generally favorable; DA lower overall but promising at low source-target similarity; no pooled AUROC reported here
caveat: Transfer depends on source-target environmental and label similarity; target-trained benchmark was overoptimistic; common terrain feature space does not establish Rwanda transferability
relevance: Supports transfer as a sensitivity analysis only, with covariate-shift diagnostics and target-event holdout; foreign inventories cannot be assumed to rescue 88 biased Rwanda records
quality_rating: High landslide-specific transfer evidence; not Rwanda
source_type: Peer-reviewed open-access article; full text read

citation: Opitz T, Bakka H, Huser R, Lombardo L. (2022). High-resolution Bayesian mapping of landslide hazard with unobserved trigger event. Annals of Applied Statistics 16:1653-1675.
region: Sicily, southern Italy; October 2009 extreme-rainfall event
data_size: 4,874 remotely sensed debris-flow landslides; 449,038 15 m grid pixels; 3,484 slope units
method: Bayesian hierarchical log-Gaussian Cox-process models with latent Gaussian spatial effects, space-varying regression, penalized-complexity priors and INLA; models an unobserved spatially varying precipitation trigger
validation_design: Multiple candidate models compared using information criteria and predictive diagnostics; exact split/holdout design and numeric scores not verified in accessed excerpt
key_metric: Information criteria and predictive diagnostics are reported; no unsupported numeric score supplied
caveat: Identifiability/confounding among latent components requires expert-informed priors; pixel-level iid effects did not improve baseline and one such model was much worse; non-replicated spatial data cannot identify the true complex intensity with high certainty
relevance: Principled alternative to binary labels for event counts and latent triggers, with uncertainty; more defensible than SMOTE for sparse spatial events but demanding
quality_rating: High landslide Bayesian evidence; preprint used because DOI host blocked
source_type: Peer-reviewed article; DOI PDF inaccessible in this run; authoritative arXiv full text read

citation: Monsieurs E, Jacobs L, Michellier C, et al. (2018). Landslide inventory for hazard assessment in a data-poor context: a regional-scale approach in a tropical African environment. Landslides 15:2195-2209.
region: LIWEAR, central section of the western branch of the East African Rift in tropical Central Africa
data_size: 143 events with known location and date spanning 1968-2016
method: Three-phase Search-Store-Validate inventory workflow combining reports, field observations and local collaboration
validation_design: Field observations and local collaboration used to validate records; no ML predictive validation
key_metric: No ML metric; authors judge the validated inventory reliable at the studied spatial and temporal resolutions
caveat: Substantial biases relate to landslide processes, impact/reporting and remote context; not a random sample; broader East African Rift rather than Rwanda-only
relevance: Closest contextual evidence that tropical African inventories can be missing-not-at-random and that improving observation may dominate algorithm choice; supports auditable data pipeline before ML
quality_rating: High contextual data-quality evidence; not an ML method paper
source_type: Peer-reviewed article; authoritative UGent record and linked full-text source read

citation: Chawla NV, Bowyer KW, Hall LO, Kegelmeyer WP. (2002). SMOTE: Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique. Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research 16:321-357.
region: No geography; generic imbalanced-classification benchmarks
data_size: Exact dataset sizes not stated in accessed abstract
method: Synthetic interpolation of minority examples plus majority undersampling; C4.5, Ripper and Naive Bayes
validation_design: Classifier experiments with ROC-space comparisons; exact split/resampling details not stated in accessed abstract
key_metric: AUC and ROC convex-hull strategy; abstract reports improvement over majority undersampling and alternative loss-ratio/class-prior settings in tested datasets
caveat: Not PU, spatial, landslide or 88-record evidence; synthetic interpolation cannot correct missing-not-at-random labels or spatial dependence; do not treat benchmark gains as Rwanda evidence
relevance: Only a baseline sensitivity experiment. Keep augmentation inside training folds, compare with no augmentation, and use geographic/event-independent evaluation; no verified GAN improvement was found
quality_rating: High original-method provenance; low direct relevance
source_type: Peer-reviewed article; accessible article landing page and full abstract read

citation: Ploton P, Mortier F, Rejou-Mechain M, et al. (2020). Spatial validation reveals poor predictive performance of large-scale ecological mapping models. Nature Communications 11:4540.
region: Central Africa across five countries, from Gabon/Cameroon toward the Democratic Republic of Congo
data_size: More than 190,000 inventory plots; about 11.8 million trees aggregated to about 60,000 1-km pixels
method: Random-forest mapping with multispectral and environmental predictors; compares random, spatial and buffered leave-one-out validation
validation_design: Random CV, spatial CV accounting for spatial autocorrelation, and buffered leave-one-out CV
key_metric: Random validation suggested more than half of biomass variation explained; spatial validation showed quasi-null predictive power
caveat: Outcome is forest biomass rather than landslides; spatial validation addresses geographic generalization, not every map-accuracy question; nevertheless demonstrates severe optimism from spatial dependence
relevance: Critical warning for 88 clustered Rwanda records: random folds may test interpolation among nearby/reporting-linked records rather than new districts or rainfall events; spatial/event blocking should be primary
quality_rating: High empirical spatial-validation evidence; indirect outcome domain
source_type: Peer-reviewed open-access article; full text read

citation: Montgomery, D.R.; Dietrich, W.E. (1994). A physically based model for the topographic control on shallow landsliding. Water Resources Research 30(4):1153-1171.
region: Tennessee Valley, California; Mettman Ridge, Oregon; Split Creek, Washington
data_size: Three basins; abstract gives no event count.
method: SHALSTAB precursor: DEM/topographic elements plus TOPOG steady-state throughflow and infinite-slope stability for cohesionless soils of constant thickness and saturated conductivity.
validation_design: Compared predictions with landslide locations mapped from aerial photographs and field work; no train/test or prospective warning validation.
key_metric: No numerical AUC or accuracy is reported; abstract says patterns were consistent with observed scars.
caveat: Authors note omitted spatial soil-property variability and bedrock flow, which control specific sites and timing; model targets shallow initiation under simplified conditions.
relevance: Causal/topographic foundation for SHALSTAB and a physically interpretable prior for low-label Rwanda modeling, but not evidence of warning skill.
quality_rating: High for original formulation and multi-basin comparison; full quantitative details were not accessible from the DOI abstract.
source_type: Peer-reviewed journal article; DOI abstract read

citation: Pack, R.T.; Tarboton, D.G.; Goodwin, C.N. (1998). The SINMAP Approach to Terrain Stability Mapping. Proceedings of the 8th Congress of the International Association of Engineering Geology, 1157-1166.
region: Kilpala watershed, northern Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada
data_size: Abstract says a landslide and terrain inventory was completed; no count reported.
method: Mechanistic infinite-slope stability plus steady-state hydrology; stability index governed mainly by specific catchment area and slope; interactively calibrated to local terrain, rainfall and soils.
validation_design: Example map produced after aerial-photo landslide and terrain inventories; no holdout or prospective warning design reported in abstract.
key_metric: No numerical validation metric reported.
caveat: Requires engineering judgment and inventory-based calibration; steady-state classes are not direct probabilities or event-time forecasts.
relevance: Interpretable low-label screening layer for Rwanda, especially topographic convergence, but calibration and inventory bias must be explicit.
quality_rating: Authoritative institutional record and original citation; conference paper with limited quantitative detail accessible.
source_type: Conference paper; institutional full abstract read

citation: Baum, R.L.; Savage, W.Z.; Godt, J.W. (2008). TRIGRS, version 2.0. USGS Open-File Report 2008-1159.
region: General regional-grid model; verification uses Minor Creek, a USGS flume experiment and Srivastava-Yeh analytical examples
data_size: No regional inventory count; analytical/experimental profile tests.
method: Transient rainfall infiltration using analytical 1-D vertical-flow solutions for homogeneous/isotropic saturated or unsaturated materials; variable rainfall step functions; optional runoff routing; cell-wise infinite-slope factor of safety.
validation_design: Reproduced published pore-pressure and factor-of-safety profiles for Iverson Minor Creek/flume examples and Srivastava-Yeh solutions; implementation verification, not independent field EWS validation.
key_metric: No field AUC, accuracy, hit-rate or false-alarm metric reported.
caveat: Sensitive to initial conditions; requires consistent grids, rainfall/infiltration history, soil strength, hydraulic parameters, soil/water-table depth and initialization. Simplifying assumptions limit generality.
relevance: Defines the data burden for a Rwanda TRIGRS EWS while providing a causal rainfall-to-factor-of-safety mechanism to constrain ML.
quality_rating: High for equations, inputs and reproducibility checks; agency verification rather than field predictive-performance validation.
source_type: USGS agency report/software documentation; page and PDF read

citation: Weidner, L.; Oommen, T.; Escobar-Wolf, R. (2018). Regional-scale back-analysis using TRIGRS in sparse data regions. Landslides 15:2343-2356.
region: Kerala, India
data_size: Two known failure events: June 2004 and July 2007.
method: TRIGRS parameterized from regional data, remote sensing and temporal back-analysis; soil thickness from slope; satellite microwave rainfall; trial-and-error cohesion, friction angle and water-table depth matched observed failure times.
validation_design: Temporal back-analysis requiring predicted and observed failure times to coincide; no independent spatial holdout reported.
key_metric: Authors explicitly report low spatial prediction accuracy and multiple solution sets; no numerical AUC/accuracy reported in accessible abstract.
caveat: Sparse and uncertain rainfall/geotechnical inputs, equifinality and low spatial accuracy; authors recommend more failures and probabilistic thresholds before EWS use.
relevance: Strongest direct sparse-inventory evidence: physics can recover plausible critical timing conditions from very few events, but spatial warning claims remain weak.
quality_rating: High relevance and peer-reviewed; exact parameter ranges and full validation details require the article full text.
source_type: Peer-reviewed journal article; DOI abstract read

citation: Liu, S.; Wang, L.; Zhang, W.; Sun, W.; Wang, Y.; Liu, J. (2024). Physics-informed optimization for a data-driven approach in landslide susceptibility evaluation. Journal of Rock Mechanics and Geotechnical Engineering 16(8):3192-3205.
region: Yunyang County, Three Gorges Reservoir area, China
data_size: 104 positive plus 104 physics-screened negative samples; 80% train and 20% validation. Bedrock-depth CNN used 6,523 boreholes, including 80 local; shear-strength data from 80 local boreholes.
method: CNN predicts bedrock depth; Scoops 3D screens negatives where factor of safety exceeds 1.5; RF susceptibility model compares physics-screened versus conventional negatives; 16 conditioning factors.
validation_design: Random 80/20 split of 208 RF samples; benchmark uses same positives and conventional negatives. CNN bedrock-depth R2=0.778, but independent split details are not fully specified.
key_metric: ROC-AUC increased from 0.67 to 0.866; conclusions report 29.25% AUC improvement; CNN bedrock-depth R2=0.778.
caveat: Negative labels are model-derived, not confirmed absences; physical accuracy depends on bedrock depth, rainfall, reservoir levels and shear-strength fields. Authors state rainfall/reservoir effects were incompletely assessed and shear strength was assumed uniform.
relevance: Concrete pattern for reducing arbitrary pseudo-absence bias with FS when event labels are few, while showing that the bottleneck can move to expensive geotechnical data and that random splits may overstate transferability.
quality_rating: High: full peer-reviewed open-access text read with explicit counts, split and metrics.
source_type: Peer-reviewed open-access article; DOI page and full text read

citation: do Pinho, T.M.; Augusto Filho, O. (2022). Landslide susceptibility mapping using the infinite slope, SHALSTAB, SINMAP, and TRIGRS models in Serra do Mar, Brazil. Journal of Mountain Science 19:1018-1036.
region: Serra do Mar, Brazil; January 2014 intense-rainfall event
data_size: Abstract says hundreds of landslides; exact count not exposed.
method: Compared infinite slope, SHALSTAB, SINMAP and TRIGRS under matched hydrogeotechnical conditions, varying soil depth, water-table height and rainfall; used granite residual-soil and unsaturated scenarios.
validation_design: Back-analysis against upper-third areas of landslide scars using validation indices; no prospective temporal split reported in accessible abstract.
key_metric: Abstract names validation indices but gives no numeric values; without rainfall models were similar, while TRIGRS at 210 mm in 2 h under unsaturated conditions was described as most reliable.
caveat: Back-analysis depends on parameter choices and one event/geological unit; not evidence of generalizable warning performance. Full quantitative details inaccessible from the DOI landing page.
relevance: Direct comparison of all requested GIS models; supports testing model agreement and rainfall scenarios rather than choosing from one score.
quality_rating: High for comparative design and qualitative findings; quantitative metrics intentionally omitted.
source_type: Peer-reviewed journal article; DOI abstract read

citation: Cheon, E.; et al. (2025). Physics-based landslide susceptibility machine learning model for mountainous solar power plants. Natural Hazards 121(17):19967-19992.
region: Jangsu-gun, Jeonbuk-do, South Korea
data_size: 136,262 numerical rainfall-infiltration, transient-seepage and slope-stability simulation points; not a field event inventory.
method: Fourteen topographic, geotechnical, hydrological, meteorological and solar-panel factors; RF, SVR and MLP emulate physically based factor of safety for fast assessment.
validation_design: Models compared on simulation data; MLP applied to a Jangsu-gun solar plant as an application check. Abstract does not specify an independent field-event test set.
key_metric: MLP R2=0.96 and mean squared error=0.001; abstract says no overfitting indicated. Sensitivity found soil strength strongly influenced factor of safety.
caveat: Simulation-trained performance is not event prediction; specialized solar-plant setting requires geotechnical parameterization and lacks demonstrated independent failure-event validation or Rwanda transferability.
relevance: Shows a surrogate-model route for fast factor-of-safety prediction, but does not show that 88 biased Rwanda records can train a reliable event classifier.
quality_rating: Moderate-high: peer-reviewed DOI verified and detailed institutional abstract read; full validation design inaccessible.
source_type: Peer-reviewed journal article; institutional full abstract read and DOI verified

citation: Monsieurs, E.; et al. (2018). Landslide inventory for hazard assessment in a data-poor context: a regional-scale approach in a tropical African environment. Landslides 15(11):2195-2209.
region: Central western branch of the East African Rift, tropical African Great Lakes context; not Rwanda-only
data_size: LIWEAR contains 143 landslide events with known location and date from 1968-2016 (48 years).
method: Search-Store-Validate inventory workflow combining field observations and local collaborations; assesses spatial/temporal accuracy, reliability and geomorphological meaning.
validation_design: Validated inventory methodology; no train/test or predictive metric in the accessible abstract.
key_metric: No AUC, accuracy or warning metric. Key finding is qualitative: substantial biases by process type, impact and remote context.
caveat: Reported-event inventories are biased by detectability, impact and remoteness; 143 dated events are not complete presence/absence labels. Geography is broader than Rwanda.
relevance: Directly supports auditing the 88-record Rwanda inventory before physics-informed ML: document search coverage, date/location confidence, process type, impact and remote-area censoring.
quality_rating: High for sparse tropical-African inventory methodology and bias diagnosis; detailed tables require full article access.
source_type: Peer-reviewed journal article; authoritative institutional abstract and citation read

citation: Ghorbanzadeh, O. et al. (2022), Landslide4Sense: Reference Benchmark Data and Deep Learning Models for Landslide Detection.
region: Iburi (Japan), Kodagu (India), Gorkha/Rasuwa (Nepal), western Taitung (Taiwan); four landslide-prone regions
data_size: 3,799 128x128 image patches; Sentinel-2 optical plus ALOS PALSAR DEM and slope; the released benchmark is also described in the competition paper as 3,799 train, 245 validation and 800 test patches
method: Pixel-wise segmentation; 11 deep models (including U-Net, ResU-Net, DeepLab variants and LinkNet) trained from scratch on Sentinel-2 plus topography
validation_design: The paper abstract states training on patches from one quarter of each study area and testing on independent patches from the other three quarters; the benchmark is geographically concentrated in four event regions, not Rwanda
key_metric: The accessible abstract verifies that ResU-Net outperformed the other tested models but does not state a numeric score; no unsupported numeric metric reported here
caveat: Single-event/site composition, manually annotated labels and severe spatial/class imbalance limit domain transfer. Native 20/60 m bands were resampled to about 10 m in the benchmark; optical cloud-free event imagery is not equivalent to humid-tropical operational coverage
relevance: Strong reference for expanding labels with Sentinel-2/topography and for enforcing region-held-out evaluation; it does not test Sentinel-1, Planet or Rwanda
quality_rating: High for benchmark description; preprint/benchmark source rather than a Rwanda validation study

citation: Ghorbanzadeh, O. et al. (2022), The Outcome of the 2022 Landslide4Sense Competition: Advanced Landslide Detection from Multisource Satellite Imagery.
region: Training sites: Hokkaido/Iburi (Japan), Kodagu (India), Rasuwa (Nepal), western Taitung (Taiwan); validation/test from other mountainous global sites
data_size: 3,799 labeled training patches plus 245 validation and 800 test patches, each 128x128 pixels; 14 layers (12 Sentinel-2 bands, ALOS PALSAR DEM and slope)
method: Competition and U-Net baseline for multisource deep semantic segmentation; all layers standardized to about 10 m/pixel
validation_design: Pixel-wise landslide F1 on the 245-patch validation set and 800-patch test set; ranking used test F1. The benchmark imagery was captured on cloud-free days after events
key_metric: Baseline U-Net: validation F1 57.82%; test F1 59.92%; corresponding test precision 52.45% and recall 69.87%. Training landslide pixels were about 2% of pixels (background about 49 times landslide pixels)
caveat: Cloud-free post-event selection creates optimistic availability relative to Rwanda's humid highlands. Patch/test performance is not an event-independent warning evaluation; external auxiliary imagery was forbidden, and the sites/events do not represent Rwanda
relevance: Useful negative evidence against assuming benchmark F1 transfers to a tiny biased Rwandan inventory; emphasizes class imbalance and geographically held-out testing
quality_rating: High; peer-reviewed IEEE paper with full arXiv text and DOI landing page verified

citation: Chen, X. et al. (2022), Deep Learning Method of Landslide Inventory Map with Imbalanced Samples in Optical Remote Sensing, Remote Sensing 14(21), 5517.
region: Bijie and Shuicheng/Fa'er/Jichang, Guizhou Province, southwest China
data_size: Bijie set: 770 landslide and 2,003 non-landslide samples, 0.8 m imagery; 70 landslide samples held out for test, remaining 700 used with augmentation; 146 landslide points in the Shuicheng generalization inventory after removing indistinct vegetation-covered points and adding newer points
method: Sentinel-2 optical imagery for Fa'er/Jichang inventory; FCN with focal loss and 5-fold cross-validation (FCN-FLK), compared with FCN, U-Net and SegNet
validation_design: For Bijie, 80/20 train/verification split within the non-test data and five-fold cross-validation for FCN-FLK; Shuicheng was a geographic generalization check. This is not a Rwanda or humid-tropical holdout
key_metric: Reported FCN-FLK results in the paper table: accuracy 0.93, recall 0.76, F1 0.62, mIoU 0.68; improvements versus plain FCN were reported as 0.08 recall, 0.09 F1 and 0.15 mIoU
caveat: The authors explicitly removed vegetation-obscured points, so the evaluated problem is easier than dense-canopy mapping. Models confused bare soil and roads with landslides; sample augmentation and random/fold splits can overstate independence
relevance: Direct evidence that imbalance handling can improve segmentation with limited labels, but it does not justify treating augmented pixels as independent records or extrapolating metrics to Rwanda
quality_rating: High; open peer-reviewed article with full publisher text verified

citation: Bhuyan, K. et al. (2023), Generating multi-temporal landslide inventories through a general deep transfer learning strategy using HR EO data, Scientific Reports 13, 162.
region: Wenchuan (China), Gorkha/Rasuwa (Nepal), Porgera (Papua New Guinea), and Kaikoura (New Zealand); includes monsoonal/tropical highland PNG
data_size: 13,423 km2 investigated across the four regions; combined multi-temporal image area reported as 70,791 km2. For Rasuwa, model-mapped landslide counts by year 2013-2019 were 35, 21, 98, 28, 18, 12 and 24
method: General deep transfer-learning approach for multi-temporal inventory generation using high-resolution EO imagery; post-event inventories were expanded through time
validation_design: Spatially independent subsets were used; predictions were assessed against manually generated ground truth using PlanetScope and RapidEye imagery, except co-seismic inventories sourced from literature
key_metric: Rasuwa table reports F1: 0.720 (2013), 0.671 (2014), 0.801 (2015 co-seismic), 0.847 (2016), 0.835 (2017), 0.826 (2018), 0.825 (2019); precision/recall were also reported per year
caveat: Authors attribute lower pre-seismic scores to shadows, cloud cover, haze, atmospheric disturbance and discoloration. False positives occurred where spectral signatures resembled landslides. Transfer is between selected event regions, not a Rwanda rainfall EWS
relevance: Shows a credible route to temporal inventory expansion and explicitly documents optical artefacts relevant to humid highlands; it is more relevant to inventory updating than to warning calibration
quality_rating: High; open full-text peer-reviewed Scientific Reports paper

citation: Meena, S.R. et al. (2023), HR-GLDD: a globally distributed dataset using generalized deep learning (DL) for rapid landslide mapping on high-resolution (HR) satellite imagery, Earth System Science Data 15, 3283-3303.
region: Ten physiographically distinct global sites in South/Southeast Asia, East Asia, South/Central America; unseen tests include Uvira, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Haiti and Indonesia
data_size: PlanetScope 3 m RGB+NIR, 128x128-pixel patches; 10 sites with five rainfall-triggered and five earthquake-triggered events. 60% train/20% validation/20% test; unseen evaluation patches: DRC 247, Haiti 461, Indonesia 403
method: Five U-Net-like deep segmentation models using manually delineated PlanetScope masks; only red, green, blue and NIR used
validation_design: Mixed-site 60/20/20 split plus individual-site tests and completely unseen-event tests; imagery was selected for minimal cloud coverage
key_metric: Average F1 about 0.7045 on the mixed HR-GLDD test; unseen-event average F1: DRC 0.5562, Haiti 0.7947, Indonesia 0.8603
caveat: Positive pixels were only 9.96% versus 90.04% background; manually delineated labels and removal of empty patches introduce selection bias. Optical-only models produced false positives on riverbeds and flat barren areas; cloud-free selection is especially optimistic for Rwanda
relevance: Best directly verified PlanetScope evidence for high-resolution inventory expansion and a useful warning that cross-region/event performance can fall sharply
quality_rating: High; open peer-reviewed ESSD full text verified

citation: Mondini, A.C. et al. (2019), Sentinel-1 SAR Amplitude Imagery for Rapid Landslide Detection, Remote Sensing 11(7), 760.
region: 32 events worldwide, including Rwanda-Bucyurabuhoro, Sri Lanka, India, Indonesia, Colombia, Japan, China and other settings
data_size: 32 known landslide events from May 2015-September 2018; 53% in Asia and about 25% in the Americas; Sentinel-1 pre/post pairs, mostly 12-24 days apart, with mean post-event delay under 10 days where occurrence date was known
method: Interpretation of Sentinel-1 C-band SAR amplitude change clusters, using VV or VV-VH SLC IW imagery; not a deep-learning model
validation_design: Case-based qualitative interpretation against reported event locations and optical imagery; no independent pixel-level ground-truth accuracy protocol
key_metric: 27 cases clearly identified, 1 identified only using prior coordinates, and 4 not visible; eight cases had enough signal to delineate borders and classify landslide type. No scalar accuracy was claimed
caveat: Performance depends on ascending/descending geometry, layover, relative slope orientation, polarization, snow/flood effects and co-registration. Rwanda-Bucyurabuhoro was clear in ascending but poorly illuminated in descending. Small valley failures and cave/covered failures were missed
relevance: Direct Sentinel-1 evidence including Rwanda: SAR can reduce cloud dependence, but it is not a universal cloud/vegetation solution and should be fused with optical/topographic context
quality_rating: High; open publisher full text verified

citation: Nasios, I. et al. (2024), Landslide Mapping from Sentinel-2 Imagery Through Change Detection, arXiv:2405.20161.
region: Haiti, Central Sulawesi (Indonesia), Luding (China), Mesetas (Colombia) and Iburi (Japan)
data_size: 34,920 manually validated landslide polygons; Sentinel-2 pre/post patches. Training/validation/test: 55,602/1,102/1,102 256x256 patches; cloud-mask filtering allowed at most 20% merged cloud cover and required visible landslide pixels
method: Bitemporal Sentinel-2 change detection with Unet-Siam-Diff, BIT, SEIFNet, TinyCD and proposed BBUnet; BBUnet fuses Sentinel-2 with DEM-derived elevation/slope/aspect
validation_design: Training used four inventories; validation and test each used half of Haiti pairs. Patches with fewer than 200 visible landslide pixels were excluded from validation/test
caveat: The authors identify imperfect/manual inventories and Sentinel-2 resolution relative to landslide size as major intrinsic problems. Cloudy images were filtered, and evaluation excluded low-landslide-content patches, so recall is not an all-scene operational estimate
relevance: Important negative/null result: even a large, heterogeneous inventory and DEM fusion yielded low F1 on a held-out event; supports conservative expectations for 88 biased Rwandan records
quality_rating: Preprint with accessible full HTML; not peer-reviewed evidence

citation: Li, et al. (2025), Landslide Hazard Mapping with Geospatial Foundation Models: Geographical Generalizability, Data Scarcity, and Band Adaptability.
region: Landslide4Sense global benchmark regions; no Rwanda study area
data_size: 4,844 128x128 patches with predefined 3,799 train, 245 validation and 800 test split; landslide pixels were 2.2% of labeled area
method: Prithvi-EO-2.0 300M/600M geospatial foundation models pretrained on 4.2 million multi-temporal HLS image sequences; fine-tuned for L4S segmentation and compared with U-Net, U-Net++, SegFormer, SwinV2-B, TransLandSeg, SatMAE and TerraMind
validation_design: Identical L4S train/validation/test splits and best-validation-loss checkpoint; the benchmark remains single-date optical plus topography and does not test Sentinel-1 or Planet
key_metric: On the L4S test set, Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M mIoU 71.30, F1 60.70, precision 57.14, recall 64.73; U-Net baseline mIoU 70.44, F1 59.66. The paper notes a reproduced TransLandSeg result of mIoU 68.30/F1 55.39 under its standard split, differing from the TransLandSeg paper's reported split
caveat: Preprint; benchmark-scale gains are modest and may not imply low-label Rwanda transfer. Spectral/interface mismatch exists (pretraining B8A vs L4S B8), class imbalance is severe, and no humid-tropical or SAR validation is provided
relevance: Most directly relevant foundation-model evidence, but it supports testing pretrained models as a hypothesis—not assuming they solve geographic shift or 88-record bias
quality_rating: Accessible preprint full HTML verified; not peer-reviewed at the accessed version

citation: UNOSAT (2023), Floods and landslides in Rwanda, product 3584 / GLIDE FL20230504RWA.
region: Rwanda
data_size: Not stated on the accessible product page
method: Satellite-imagery-based live web map of floods and landslides; detailed sensor, labels and processing are not stated on the accessible page
validation_design: Not stated
key_metric: Not reported; no accuracy metric inferred
caveat: Accessible page provides only publication date (11 May 2023), product ID and a map/download link; it does not document cloud/vegetation handling, ground truth, sample count or validation
relevance: Direct Rwanda operational context and a plausible source of event polygons, but insufficient by itself for ML training or evidence of mapping accuracy
quality_rating: Authoritative agency product page; methodological details inaccessible from the page

citation: Guzzetti, F., Gariano, S.L., Rianna, G., et al. (2020). Geographical landslide early warning systems. Earth-Science Reviews, 200, 102973.
region: 26 regional, national, and global LEWS worldwide; 1977–August 2019
data_size: 26 systems reviewed; the paper does not provide a pooled event-level sample for all systems
method: Critical review of nine assumptions underpinning landslide forecasting and early warning; compares rainfall, meteorological-model, radar, satellite, susceptibility, rainfall-threshold, slope-stability, and soil-water-balance approaches.
validation_design: Most reviewed systems had some form of verification, but the review states there was no accepted standard for checking LEWS performance or forecasting skill; no universal independent-validation result is supplied.
key_metric: No pooled POD/FAR metric. Verified synthesis: operational forecasting of weather-induced landslides is feasible; systems commonly use two rainfall-information sources and different forecast-model families.
caveat: Review-level evidence is heterogeneous and not a common benchmark; catalog, spatial scale, warning definitions, and validation designs differ across systems.
relevance: Best high-level benchmark for deciding what an operational Rwanda EWS must contain and why cross-system ML metric transfer is unsafe.
quality_rating: High—peer-reviewed Earth-Science Reviews synthesis; no pooled performance estimate.

citation: Piciullo, L., Calvello, M., & Ranieri, G. (2020). Standards for the performance assessment of territorial landslide early warning systems. Landslides.
region: Piemonte, Italy SMART case; comparisons include Hong Kong, Rio de Janeiro, Southern California, and Emilia-Romagna SIGMA
data_size: Review audit: 115 rainfall-threshold papers (38 independent validation, 31 calibration-set validation, 46 no predictive evaluation). SMART: >400 gauges over 25,873 km2; 10 warning zones; January 2008–December 2016; 3,287 daily duration-matrix elements per zone.
method: EDuMaP duration-matrix assessment of multi-level territorial warnings; compares with standard 2x2 contingency tables. SMART uses empirical intensity-duration thresholds and three warning levels tied to estimated landslide counts.
validation_design: SMART evaluation uses recorded landslide and warning events over 2008–2016; the paper emphasizes that independent validation is uncommon and that 2x2 tables omit warning levels, multiple landslides, and error severity.
key_metric: SMART: in 6/10 zones EI_A was <50%; serious missed-alert probability exceeded 10% in 6/10 zones; the missed/false-alert balance (MFB) met the <25% operational-efficiency recommendation in only 1/10 zones. Comparative Hong Kong values reported from Cheung et al.: EI_A 61% for SWIRLS Landslip Alert and 78% for standard landslip warning; MFB 33% and 0%. Comparative Rio values from cited EDuMaP work: EI_A 75% Guanabara and 66% Zona Sul; MFB 14.5% and 3.4%.
caveat: Metrics are warning-zone/day and severity-dependent, not directly equivalent to pixel-level POD/FPR. Comparisons reuse published studies with different definitions; high true negatives can inflate conventional efficiency/odds metrics.
relevance: Directly informs a skeptical evaluation plan: define event and warning units, include multiple warning levels, report missed versus false-alert costs, and avoid accuracy dominated by negatives.
quality_rating: High—peer-reviewed methods paper with an explicit multi-level territorial evaluation.

citation: Kirschbaum, D., Stanley, T., & Zhou, Y. (2018). Satellite-based assessment of rainfall-triggered landslide hazard for situational awareness. Earth’s Future, 6, 505–523.
region: Global tropics and middle latitudes; separate Nepal validation inventory
data_size: Global Landslide Catalog (GLC) had >9,500 reported events (2007 onward). Retrospective evaluation: TMPA 2007–2016 and IMERG 2014–2017. Nepal Petley inventory: 384 validation points for 2007–2016 TMPA and 82 for 2014–2016 IMERG.
method: LHASA v1 heuristic decision-tree nowcast combining static susceptibility variables with near-real-time satellite precipitation; moderate and high hazard categories; spatial buffers account for reported-location uncertainty.
validation_design: Retrospective comparison of daily nowcasts with GLC over 1-, 3-, and 7-day windows; also tested a separate Nepal database. This is catalog-based validation, not a prospective randomized or unbiased event sample.
key_metric: Global overall FPR: 1% for moderate hazard and 0.2% for high hazard. Nepal TMPA TPR for moderate hazard: 32%, 47%, 58% at 1/3/7 days; high hazard: 22%, 33%, 40%. Nepal IMERG moderate: 40%, 50%, 60%; high: 26%, 30%, 39%. Nepal FPR values in the reported table were 3% (moderate) and 1% (high) for TMPA, and 3% and 2% for IMERG.
