caveat: GLC is media/report based and explicitly biased by language, population/infrastructure proximity, impacts, political/reporting conditions, and location uncertainty; model did not predict most GLC landslides. Near-real-time nowcast is not a demonstrated actionable lead-time evaluation; rainfall-triggered processes only.
relevance: A strong cautionary analogue for Rwanda: even a global operational baseline has substantial selection bias and incomplete recall; evaluate records and negatives as an observation process, not ground truth.
quality_rating: High—peer-reviewed, open full text, with explicit validation tables and catalog-bias discussion.

citation: Khan, S., Kirschbaum, D., Amatya, P., et al. (2022). Global Landslide Forecasting System for Hazard Assessment and Situational Awareness. Frontiers in Earth Science, 10, 878996.
region: Global LHASA-Forecast product; validation uses seven rainfall-induced mapped inventories
data_size: Seven mapped rainfall-induced landslide inventories for model validation; training years 2015–2018 and evaluation years 2019–2020. The accessible article text does not state a single event count in the summary section.
method: LHASA v2 XGBoost model using daily IMERG rainfall/antecedent rainfall, SMAP soil wetness and snow mass, slope, lithology, and distance to active faults; 30-arcsecond grid; outputs updated four times daily.
validation_design: Temporal split: 2015–2018 development and 2019–2020 evaluation; seven high-resolution mapped inventories. Dates/locations without recorded landslides were assumed non-occurrence and a random sample used for model development.
key_metric: Reported aggregated true-positive rate was 93% for v2 versus 45% for v1.1. No FAR/FPR is reported in the verified article text used here.
caveat: The negative class is partly constructed from unrecorded locations/dates, so selection and label bias remain central; inventories assume mapped landslides in an event boundary were rainfall-triggered and do not distinguish source from deposition. Aggregated TPR is not a Rwanda-transferable estimate and no actionable lead-time metric is established here.
relevance: Useful ML operational precedent, but its validation design demonstrates why a small biased Rwanda inventory cannot justify headline TPR without independent spatial/temporal testing and label-bias analysis.
quality_rating: High—peer-reviewed open-access paper; important caveats are stated in the article.

citation: Segoni, S., Piciullo, L., & Gariano, S.L. (2018). A Regional-Scale Landslide Warning System Based on 20 Years of Operational Experience. Water, 10(10), 1297.
region: Emilia-Romagna, Italy; SIGMA regional system
data_size: Calibration/experience table reports 180 landslides for incomplete 2000–2003 prototypal calibration, 888 for 2004–2007, and 1,652 for 2004–2010; counts refer to calibration datasets and are not a simple independent test sample.
method: Daily rainfall-threshold system: short intense events use 2-sigma rainfall over 1–10 days in the prototype; long-duration events use 1.5-sigma over 10–365 days. Later versions customize thresholds by territorial unit, add seasonality, snow processes, susceptibility, and soil moisture.
validation_design: Iterative operational calibration and error analysis across model versions; the paper advocates constant validation but the reported comparisons are not a clean single untouched holdout. Performance indicators are likelihood ratios and false/missed-alert counts.
key_metric: Likelihood ratio increased 8.38 to 16.43 to 17.01 across reported versions. In 2004–2007, false alarms fell from 845 to 562 after algorithm/threshold updates. A soil-moisture alternative reduced false alarms 15% and missed alarms 22% in the reported test.
caveat: Performance is model-version and dataset dependent; likelihood ratio can be sensitive to contingency definitions and true negatives. The system forecasts regional warning conditions, not individual-slope failure probability; no directly comparable POD/FAR/lead-time result is established in the accessible text.
relevance: Shows that low/fragmented archives can support a transparent operational baseline, but only through long-term updating, spatial customization, and repeated error analysis—not a one-shot high-capacity ML claim.
quality_rating: High—peer-reviewed open-access operational history with explicit calibration counts and error metrics.

citation: Segoni, S., Piciullo, L., & Gariano, S.L. (2015). An operational landslide early warning system at regional scale based on space–time-variable rainfall thresholds. Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences, 15, 853–861.
region: Tuscany, Italy (23,000 km2)
data_size: More than 300 automated rain gauges; 25 independent alert zones. The paper abstract does not give a landslide-event count.
method: Space-time-variable intensity-duration thresholds using real-time rain-gauge data and LAMI limited-area rainfall forecasts, implemented in a civil-protection WebGIS with zone-specific monitoring and forecast views.
validation_design: The verified article page describes operational setup and forecast/monitoring workflow but does not provide a quantified independent validation sample in the abstract text accessed here.
key_metric: No POD/FAR/accuracy metric reported in the verified abstract. Forecast display supports lead times up to 48 hours; this is a forecast horizon, not necessarily realized evacuation lead time.
caveat: No event-level performance metrics should be inferred from the system description. Threshold and forecast errors, spatial aggregation, and actual decision/response time are not quantified in the accessible abstract.
relevance: Concrete example of an operational, low-complexity regional design with explicit forecast horizon and alert zoning; useful comparator for an 88-record Rwanda baseline.
quality_rating: High for operational architecture—peer-reviewed NHESS paper; quantitative validation details were inaccessible in the fetched abstract.

citation: Calvello, M., d’Orsi, R.N., Piciullo, L., et al. (2015). The Rio de Janeiro early warning system for rainfall-induced landslides: Analysis of performance for the years 2010–2013. International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction, 12, 3–15.
region: Municipality of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil (Alerta-Rio)
data_size: Performance period 2010–2013; city divided into four alert zones (Guanabara, Zona Sul, Sepetiba, Jacarepaguà). The accessible DOI text does not expose a single total landslide-event count.
method: Operational system combines rainfall and landslide warnings; four landslide warning levels (low, medium, high, very high) tied to expected spatial landslide density; evaluates rainfall events, landslide events, and warning levels.
validation_design: Retrospective performance analysis of correlation models and rainfall thresholds for 2010–2013; four warning zones and multi-level warnings. The accessible landing text does not provide the full numeric contingency tables.
key_metric: No numeric POD/FAR is asserted from the accessible DOI extract. The paper explicitly frames efficiency as reducing false and missed alerts; related EDuMaP comparison values are reported in Piciullo et al. (2020), not substituted here as if they were this paper’s directly displayed results.
caveat: Municipal Brazil is not equivalent to Brazil’s national CEMADEN operation; warning-level and spatial-density definitions limit direct comparison with binary ML metrics. Full tables/lead-time values were inaccessible in the DOI extract.
relevance: Brazilian operational precedent showing why warning levels, spatial density, and false/missed-alert analysis matter; it should not be used as evidence for CEMADEN national performance.
quality_rating: High—peer-reviewed DOI landing page verifies study scope and design; numeric performance tables were inaccessible.

citation: World Meteorological Organization (WMO). WMO and the Early Warnings for All Initiative (official operational guidance page).
region: Global, with emphasis on countries and territories lacking adequate MHEWS
data_size: Not applicable; policy/guidance page reports global capacity indicators rather than a landslide validation dataset.
method: People-centred end-to-end framework with four pillars: disaster-risk knowledge; detection/observation/monitoring/analysis/forecasting; warning dissemination/communication; preparedness/response. WMO leads Pillar 2.
validation_design: Guidance emphasizes real-time data sharing, operational centres, standards, proactive action, governance, and capacity building; it does not prescribe a landslide-specific POD/FAR experiment.
key_metric: No landslide POD/FAR. Page reports system-capacity indicators, including only 67% of WMO Members reporting 24/7 warning services and 56% using hazard/exposure/vulnerability data in forecasts; these are not model skill metrics.
caveat: Multi-hazard governance guidance is not a landslide model validation protocol. Capacity indicators are self-reported/global and cannot establish Rwanda model performance.
relevance: Prevents an ML-only framing: a technically accurate alert that is not communicated, trusted, or actionable is not an operational EWS; supports low-tech redundancy and sustainable data/governance planning.
quality_rating: High—official WMO/UN Early Warnings for All source.

citation: Devkota, S., et al. (2023). Developing Community-Based Landslide Early Warning System for Data Scarce Geographical Areas—A Case of Neelakantha Municipality, Dhading, Nepal. SSRN preprint.
region: Neelakantha Municipality, Dhading District, central Nepal; pilot area about 200 km2 and vulnerable catchment about 12 km2
data_size: 162 field-verified landslides; occurrence dates identified for 33 previously triggered landslides; daily and 5-day antecedent rainfall used. Automated rain gauges, soil-moisture sensors, and extensometers were installed.
method: Community-maintained inventory, susceptibility mapping, UAV and geotechnical investigation, factor-of-safety modelling, rainfall-threshold development, automated sensors, and a dashboard integrating government rain forecasts.
validation_design: The abstract describes development toward prediction and advance alerts but does not report an independent holdout, prospective trial, POD, FAR, calibration score, or realized lead-time evaluation.
key_metric: No verified predictive performance metric or realized warning lead time reported in the accessible abstract.
caveat: Preprint status; only 33 dated landslides underpin rainfall-threshold development; pilot design and sensor/dashboard operation are not evidence of sustained operational performance. Community data may still have detection/reporting bias.
relevance: Close low-resource analogue: demonstrates how to turn sparse records into a transparent, sensor-assisted baseline while making clear that data assembly and operational testing precede claims of ML generalization.
quality_rating: Moderate—real, accessible preprint with specific sample counts, but not peer reviewed and without performance validation.

citation: UNDRR (2024). Developing a participatory landslide early warning system: The Inform@Risk project in Colombia.
region: Medellín, Colombia; informally urbanized, landslide-prone area
data_size: Four-year interdisciplinary project ending December 2022; no event-count or sensor-sample total stated on the authoritative case-study page.
method: Site-specific participatory EWS combining academia, local government, civil society, private sector, and local community; culturally and spatially adapted; transition planning for municipal operation.
validation_design: Preliminary prototype only; municipality was operating the system in test mode. The page reports no independent predictive validation, POD/FAR, or realized lead-time metric.
key_metric: No verified quantitative performance metric.
caveat: The project had not yet reached a full-functioning EWS; governance, illegal armed actors, COVID-19, bureaucracy, and trust/continuity challenges affected implementation. Do not describe it as a proven operational ML system.
relevance: Low-resource and people-centred Colombian example: operational readiness includes governance, trust, continuity, and test-mode evaluation, not only a hazard classifier.
quality_rating: Moderate—official UNDRR case study with explicit prototype/test-mode caveat, but no quantitative validation.

citation: Kuradusenge, M.; Kumaran, S.; Zennaro, M. (2020). Rainfall-Induced Landslide Prediction Using Machine Learning Models: The Case of Ngororero District, Rwanda. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 17(11), 4147.
region: Ngororero District, western/northwestern Rwanda
data_size: 3,970 daily rainfall/non-rainfall instances assembled for 2011–2018; rainfall records came from Sovu and Muramba stations. The article does not state the number of positive landslide-labeled rows in the extracted methods.
method: Random forest and logistic regression using rainfall, antecedent 5-day rainfall, slope, soil type/depth and land cover; missing values filled with medians.
validation_design: Random 5-fold CV plus many random train/test ratios (0.80/0.20 through 0.55/0.45); final comparison used a 65% train/35% test ratio. No spatial block, future-time, season, or leave-one-event-out validation was reported.
key_metric: With antecedent rainfall, abstract AUC was 0.995 (RF) and 0.997 (LR); reported table values include recall 95.19%/96.15%, specificity 97.64%/98.38%, FPR 2.35%/1.61%, and FNR 4.80%/3.84% (RF/LR). Accuracy was also reported.
caveat: The authors acknowledge class imbalance but still evaluate daily rows with random folds/splits. Serially related days, repeated weather-station information and event clustering mean these rows are not independent events; the paper did not test this dependence, calibration, PR-AUC, Brier, POD/FAR/CSI/TSS, or operational future performance. Its impressive random-split AUC is therefore not evidence of spatial/temporal EWS generalization.
relevance: Closest Rwanda ML precedent: documents what a conventional random validation can report, and why an 88-record event-level study should not copy it without grouped spatial/temporal validation.
quality_rating: High for reported facts: full PMC article read; limitations about dependence are an evidence-based interpretation of its documented design, not claims made by the authors.

citation: Patton, A.I.; Roering, J.J.; Jacobs, A.; Korup, O.; Mirus, B.B. (2023). Landslide initiation thresholds in data-sparse regions: application to landslide early warning criteria in Sitka, Alaska, USA. Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences, 23, 3261–3280.
region: Sitka, Alaska, USA
data_size: Five landslide-triggering precipitation events and more than 6,000 non-triggering rainfall days, 2002–2020; timing was known within 12 h or finer resolution.
method: 136 frequentist/Bayesian logistic- and Poisson-regression models using precipitation accumulations from 1 h to 2 weeks; warning thresholds were then selected.
validation_design: Leave-one-landslide-event-out/jackknife sensitivity analysis; also trained a frequentist model on an earlier subset containing three of five events and tested it on the later two events. Compared against historical daily landslide frequency.
key_metric: The paper reports model selection/threshold results and says the selected model outperformed the historical-frequency reference and correctly predicted the two later events in the 3-of-5 test. It does not report POD, FAR, CSI, TSS, PR-AUC or Brier in the verified sections.
caveat: Only five event dates; the authors note higher uncertainty at high precipitation values. The 3-of-5 result is encouraging but extremely low-power and site-specific; it is not evidence that an 88-record biased inventory can support many tuned models. Antecedent precipitation did not improve fit relative to 3 h triggering precipitation in this dataset (a documented null finding).
relevance: Best directly verified precedent here for leave-one-event-out and future-event holdout under a scant event record, plus an explicit climatological benchmark and a negative feature finding.
quality_rating: High: full NHESS article read; event counts, validation design and null finding verified.

citation: Roberts, D.R., et al. (2017). Cross-validation strategies for data with temporal, spatial, hierarchical, or phylogenetic structure. Ecography, 40, 913–929.
region: Not a landslide geography; general structured ecological data
data_size: No single landslide sample; review, simulations and case studies.
method: Reviews random versus non-random/block CV for dependence in space, time, groups and predictor space; explains how structured non-causal covariates can overfit without obvious residual correlation.
validation_design: Recommends contiguous spatial blocks for new locations, contiguous temporal blocks for future periods, and blocking by the relevant group/dependence structure; random CV may be reasonable only when prediction remains within the same structure and no extrapolation is intended.
key_metric: Focus is prediction-error estimation and model-selection implications; no single landslide metric or event count is reported in the verified source.
caveat: Blocking can induce extrapolation and overestimate error if its geometry does not match the deployment target; no universal block design exists. It does not prescribe a landslide-specific season/event scheme or a permutation-test procedure.
relevance: Core justification for spatial blocks, temporal holdout and leave-one-group/event-out designs for biased 88-record data; also explains why checking only residual autocorrelation is insufficient.
quality_rating: High: authoritative publisher article read; DOI and recommendations verified. Author string is abbreviated here because the extracted page exposed the lead authors and title but not the complete author list.

citation: Valavi, R.; Elith, J.; Lahoz-Monfort, J.J.; Guillera-Arroita, G. (2019). blockCV: An R package for generating spatially or environmentally separated folds for k-fold cross-validation of species distribution models. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 10, 225–232.
region: General spatial modelling; no landslide geography
data_size: No data included in the article; package/tool methodology.
method: Provides spatial blocks, spatial buffers and environmental blocks; supports random/systematic/checkerboard allocation and fold-balance constraints. Uses variograms/autocorrelation ranges in predictors to inform block or buffer size.
validation_design: Non-random folds keep all observations in held-out spatial/environmental units out of training; buffering can ensure no test point abuts training data. Block size should reflect autocorrelation range and the intended extrapolation task.
key_metric: No single performance metric or landslide result; purpose is to generate valid folds and inspect fold distribution.
caveat: Choosing block size is difficult and can depend on fitted residuals, raw predictors or the deployment question; no data were included. It does not solve sparse-event uncertainty or prescribe a metric suite.
relevance: Concrete implementation path for spatial-block CV around 88 biased records, including buffer distance and fold-balance checks so rare positives are not absent from a test fold.
quality_rating: High: full DOI landing/article text read; method and caveats verified.

citation: Milne, P. (2022). Methodological and conceptual challenges in rare and severe event forecast verification. Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences, 22, 539–556.
region: General rare/severe natural hazards; avalanche/tornado examples, with landslides in scope
data_size: Illustrative Finley tornado example: 2,803 forecasts, 51 tornado occurrences and 2,752 non-occurrences; not a landslide dataset.
method: Critical review of binary rare/severe event verification and contingency-table skill measures, with an avalanche nearest-neighbour example.
validation_design: Not a CV study; emphasizes that score choice must reflect rare-event base rates and the intended scope of the forecast. It argues for skill rather than raw accuracy.
key_metric: Shows the accuracy paradox (96.6% accuracy in the illustrative tornado example) and argues that the Peirce skill score, equivalent to TSS/KSS in the binary setting, is the only reviewed skill score meeting its three adequacy constraints, possibly augmented by accuracy as a tiebreaker.
caveat: This is a theoretical argument, not an empirical landslide benchmark; it does not establish that TSS alone is sufficient for probabilistic/calibrated EWS or replace POD/FAR/CSI/reliability analysis.
relevance: Supports reporting TSS/Peirce skill rather than accuracy alone for rare landslides and explains why changing thresholds can reverse model rankings; useful for skeptical interpretation of 88-record scores.
quality_rating: High: full NHESS article read; example counts and main conclusion verified.

citation: Saito, T.; Rehmsmeier, M. (2015). The Precision-Recall Plot Is More Informative than the ROC Plot When Evaluating Binary Classifiers on Imbalanced Datasets. PLOS ONE, 10(3), e0118432.
region: General binary classification; bioinformatics simulation and miRNA examples
data_size: Simulations used 1,000 positives plus 1,000 negatives (balanced) or 1,000 positives plus 10,000 negatives (imbalanced), iterated 1,000 times; real examples T1 had 819 positives/11,060 negatives and T2 had 111/13,444.
method: Compared ROC/ROC-AUC, precision-recall curves and related evaluation measures using simulated score distributions and re-analysis of miRNA classifiers.
validation_design: Metric comparison under controlled class imbalance and two real datasets; not spatial/temporal CV and not landslide-specific.
key_metric: Concludes PRC is more informative for strongly imbalanced data because it evaluates the fraction of true positives among positive predictions; ROC visual interpretation can be deceptive under imbalance. No landslide metric values are reported.
caveat: The setting is bioinformatics and the paper concerns curve interpretation, not dependence-aware resampling, calibration or operational costs. PR-AUC is not a substitute for threshold-specific false-alarm costs or event-level validation.
relevance: Justifies adding PR curves/AUPRC to ROC-AUC for rare landslide events, while retaining POD/FAR/CSI/TSS at explicit warning thresholds.
quality_rating: High: full DOI-linked PLOS article read; sample sizes and conclusions verified.

citation: Gneiting, T.; Balabdaoui, F.; Raftery, A.E. (2007). Probabilistic forecasts, calibration and sharpness. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 69, 243–268.
region: General probabilistic forecasting; illustrative wind-speed forecasts in the US Pacific Northwest
data_size: No landslide/event sample; methodological paper with a wind-speed forecast illustration.
method: Defines calibration as statistical consistency between predictive distributions and observations, and sharpness as concentration of forecasts; develops calibration plots/diagnostics and proper scoring-rule use.
validation_design: Recommends combining calibration/sharpness diagnostics with cross-validation or time-series evaluation; does not prescribe landslide spatial blocks or event leave-out.
key_metric: Supports proper scoring rules and reliability/calibration diagnostics; for binary landslide probabilities this motivates Brier score plus reliability diagrams, but the article page does not provide a Rwanda or landslide Brier value.
caveat: General probabilistic-forecast theory; calibration diagrams and Brier estimates can be unstable with very few positive events, so an 88-record study should show uncertainty and event grouping rather than rely on one aggregate score. The source itself is not a landslide study.
relevance: Provides the evidence basis for evaluating probability quality, not just ranking/AUC or threshold classification, which is essential for an operational EWS.
quality_rating: High: authoritative publisher article read; citation, DOI and calibration/sharpness claims verified.

citation: National Center for Atmospheric Research/Developmental Testbed Center. Verification Statistics for Binary Categorical Forecasts (METplus Practical Session Guide, version 5.0).
region: General meteorological binary forecasts; examples include tornadoes and 100-year floods
data_size: No study sample; definitions and illustrative rare-event discussion.
method: Contingency-table verification guidance for deterministic binary forecasts.
validation_design: Not a resampling or CV protocol; defines how to score an already specified forecast/observation sequence.
key_metric: Defines POD/hit rate as event detection, says POD is useful for rare events; defines POFD/false-alarm rate, FAR as false yes forecasts among yes forecasts, and CSI/threat score as hits divided by hits+false alarms+misses while ignoring correct negatives. It warns accuracy is misleading for rare events.
caveat: The page does not cover spatial blocks, temporal/event holdout, permutation tests, calibration/Brier or PR-AUC; it is a metric-definition resource, not evidence of model performance.
relevance: Operationally clear definitions for POD, FAR and CSI and a direct warning against accuracy for rare landslides; pair with TSS/Peirce and probabilistic reliability rather than use any one score alone.
quality_rating: High for definitions: full DTC guidance page read. The NOAA glossary PDF was not used because extraction was inaccessible/truncated.

citation: Kuradusenge, M., Kumaran, S., & Zennaro, M. (2020). Rainfall-Induced Landslide Prediction Using Machine Learning Models: The Case of Ngororero District, Rwanda. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 17(11), 4147.
region: Ngororero District, northwestern Rwanda; 2011–2018
data_size: 3,970 rainfall/non-rainfall instances; combinatorial expansion reported as 535,950 rows (3,970 × 5 slope × 3 soil × 3 depth × 3 land-cover categories). The paper does not state an 88-record set or the positive-label count.
method: Random forest and logistic regression using daily rainfall, 5-day antecedent rainfall, slope, soil type/depth, and land cover; median imputation; RF feature importance; logistic coefficients.
validation_design: 5-fold cross-validation plus multiple random train/test ratios; selected 65% train/35% test for both models. No spatial or temporal holdout, external validation, calibration set, conformal prediction, or uncertainty interval evaluation is reported.
key_metric: With antecedent rainfall, reported cross-validation accuracy 98.74% RF and 98.79% LR; Table 4 reports RF/LR recall 95.19%/96.15%, specificity 97.64%/98.38%, FPR 2.35%/1.61%, FNR 4.80%/3.84%; ROC-AUC 0.995/0.997. These are discrimination/classification metrics, not calibration metrics.
caveat: The expanded rows are not independent real landslide observations; the paper acknowledges label imbalance but does not quantify positive count in the accessible text. Two gauges plus IDW interpolation, administrative incident reporting, selected rainy days, random splits, and no calibration/shift analysis leave substantial leakage, prevalence, spatial-transfer, and temporal-dependence concerns. High AUC/FNR cannot establish reliable alert probabilities.
relevance: Direct warning against treating a small, biased incident inventory plus synthetic/combinatorial expansion as calibrated risk. For Rwanda, require temporal/spatial blocked validation, held-out probability calibration, and explicit uncertainty/false-alarm analysis before alert deployment.
quality_rating: High for documenting this paper’s own data/design/results because full open text was read; low-to-moderate for operational performance because of the design limitations.

citation: Angelopoulos, A. N., & Bates, S. (2023). Conformal Prediction: A Gentle Introduction. Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning, 16(4), 494–591.
region: General methodology; illustrative ImageNet classification example, not Rwanda
data_size: Methodological source, not one application cohort; the tutorial’s illustrative example uses approximately 500 fresh calibration/holdout points.
method: Split conformal prediction: fit any predictor, compute nonconformity scores on an independent calibration set, and threshold scores at an adjusted empirical quantile to produce prediction sets/intervals.
validation_design: The theorem assumes calibration and test pairs are i.i.d./exchangeable. The text distinguishes marginal coverage from conditional subgroup coverage and discusses covariate-shift weighting and drift as restricted/active areas.
key_metric: Finite-sample marginal coverage: P(Ytest ∈ C(Xtest)) ≥ 1−α, with the displayed finite-sample upper bound 1−α+1/(n+1) in the standard setup. No Rwanda performance metric is reported.
caveat: Coverage is marginal and depends on exchangeability; it does not guarantee village-, season-, slope-, or rare-event-specific coverage. With only 88 biased records, a calibration split leaves few effective points and quantile resolution is coarse; spatial/temporal shift and biased labels can break nominal validity.
relevance: Best-supported basis for a transparent uncertainty layer around an existing Rwanda classifier, but only after designing an independent calibration set and testing spatial/temporal exchangeability. For binary alerts, conformal prediction yields sets such as {no-landslide}, {landslide}, or {both/uncertain}, not automatically a calibrated probability.
quality_rating: High: full open HTML source read; foundational methodological evidence.

citation: Romano, Y., Patterson, E., & Candès, E. (2019). Conformalized Quantile Regression. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32.
region: General regression methodology; benchmark regression datasets, not Rwanda
data_size: No single application sample size is stated in the accessible abstract/full-text extraction; experiments use multiple popular regression datasets.
method: Conformalized quantile regression combines quantile regression with conformal calibration to adapt interval width to heteroscedasticity rather than using constant/weakly varying-width intervals.
validation_design: The paper establishes a finite-sample valid-coverage guarantee under the conformal exchangeability setup and compares interval efficiency with other conformal methods on benchmark datasets.
key_metric: The abstract verifies valid finite-sample coverage and that intervals tend to be shorter than competing conformal methods; no exact benchmark numbers are used here.
caveat: Finite-sample validity is marginal under the relevant exchangeability assumptions; adaptive width does not solve biased labels, spatial dependence, covariate shift, or rare-event subgroup coverage. It is primarily a regression-interval method, so direct binary-alert use requires careful score/set design.
relevance: Useful if Rwanda forecasts rainfall-triggered displacement, rainfall thresholds, or continuous hazard intensity; interval width can become an ‘uncertain/monitor’ state rather than forcing a binary alarm. It cannot manufacture information absent from 88 biased records.
quality_rating: High: authoritative arXiv abstract and NeurIPS paper source opened; exact numerical benchmark metrics intentionally omitted.
source_type: Peer-reviewed conference paper and open preprint

citation: Guo, C., Pleiss, G., Sun, Y., & Weinberger, K. Q. (2017). On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks. Proceedings of ICML 34, PMLR 70, 1321–1330.
region: Image and document classification datasets; not Rwanda
data_size: Multiple image/document classification datasets; no single N is stated in the accessible abstract page.
method: Evaluates confidence calibration and post-processing methods, especially temperature scaling, on modern neural-network classifiers.
validation_design: Empirical comparisons across classification datasets; the accessible paper abstract does not expose a full split-by-split protocol, so no stronger validation claim is made here.
key_metric: The verified abstract reports that modern neural networks can be poorly calibrated and that temperature scaling is often effective; no exact ECE/Brier numbers are reported here.
caveat: Results concern neural classifiers and do not establish that temperature scaling works with an 88-record, biased landslide inventory. Post-hoc calibration needs independent held-out data and can fail under prevalence, spatial, seasonal, or sensor shift.
relevance: Supports treating LR/RF/NN scores as uncalibrated until checked. For Rwanda, use held-out reliability diagrams, Brier/log loss, calibration slope/intercept, and decision-threshold analysis rather than reporting AUC alone.
quality_rating: High: full PMLR abstract page read; exact numerical results omitted where not visible in the accessed text.

citation: Kuleshov, V., Fenner, N., & Ermon, S. (2018). Accurate Uncertainties for Deep Learning Using Calibrated Regression. arXiv:1807.00263.
region: General regression/time-series/RL methodology; not Rwanda
data_size: Bayesian linear regression, feedforward and recurrent neural networks; exact dataset sizes are not stated in the accessed abstract.
method: A calibration procedure for predictive regression distributions/credible intervals, inspired by Platt scaling; the abstract states it can calibrate any regression algorithm given enough data.
validation_design: Evaluated on regression models and time-series forecasting/model-based reinforcement-learning tasks; the accessible abstract does not provide split sizes.
key_metric: The abstract reports consistently well-calibrated credible intervals and improved performance on the evaluated forecasting/RL tasks; no exact numeric metrics are used here.
caveat: ‘Given enough data’ is decisive for an 88-record setting; calibration cannot correct biased labels or non-exchangeable spatial/temporal sampling. Credible intervals from a misspecified model are not automatically calibrated after deployment shift.
relevance: Conceptual support for calibrating predictive intervals or probabilities after model fitting, but the small Rwanda sample likely makes calibration noisy and should be reported with uncertainty and sensitivity analyses.
quality_rating: Moderate-to-high: authoritative arXiv source read; exact numerical results intentionally omitted.
source_type: Open preprint; presented at ICML 2018 according to the source record

citation: Lakshminarayanan, B., Pritzel, A., & Blundell, C. (2017). Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30.
region: Classification/regression benchmarks and ImageNet; not Rwanda
data_size: Multiple benchmark datasets and ImageNet; no single N is stated on the accessible abstract page.
method: Train multiple independently initialized models and use the ensemble predictive distribution/spread as a practical uncertainty estimate; compared with approximate Bayesian neural networks.
validation_design: Experiments cover classification and regression benchmarks and test examples from known and unknown distributions to assess dataset-shift robustness.
key_metric: The verified abstract reports well-calibrated uncertainty estimates comparable to or better than approximate Bayesian NNs and higher uncertainty on out-of-distribution examples; no exact numeric metrics are used here.
caveat: Ensemble spread is a model-disagreement signal, not a guaranteed probability or coverage interval. With 88 biased records, members may share the same sampling/label bias; low spread can reflect shared blind spots. Calibration and spatial/temporal external validation remain necessary.
relevance: A practical diagnostic for a Rwanda EWS: use member disagreement to flag ‘uncertain—do not automate escalation,’ but do not map raw spread directly to probability without held-out calibration.
quality_rating: High: official NeurIPS abstract page read; exact numerical results intentionally omitted.

citation: Calvello, M., d’Orsi, R., Piciullo, L., Paes, N., & Magalhães, M. (2015). The Rio de Janeiro early warning system for rainfall-induced landslides: Analysis of performance for the years 2010–2013. International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction, 12, 3–15.
region: Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; citywide Alerta-Rio system; 2010–2013
data_size: 132 landslide events; 714 landslide occurrences; 31 high/very-high alert phases across four alert zones.
method: Retrospective comparison of rainfall events, landslide events/occurrences, warning levels, alert phases, durations, and zones; four warning levels: low, medium, high, very high.
validation_design: Operational retrospective performance analysis, not an ML validation study. Alert phase was defined as high or very high; false alert was conservatively defined as an alert phase with no recorded landslide occurrence.
key_metric: 502/714 landslides occurred during alert phases. False-alert ratios reported: Guanabara 3/14; Zona Sul 5/8 = 0.63; Sepetiba 1/2; Jacarepaguà 3/7; overall lower-bound false-alert ratio 12/31 ≈ 0.39 under the paper’s conservative definition. Alerts were frequently long, including an April 2010 event lasting more than 110 hours in all zones.
caveat: A ‘false alert’ based on zero occurrences is conservative because high/very-high levels imply diffuse/widespread density, not necessarily at least one event; event reporting and spatial heterogeneity affect results. The study is Rio-specific and cannot set Rwanda’s acceptable rate.
relevance: Direct evidence that alert-level design must balance missed events, false alarms, alert duration, spatial aggregation, and action thresholds. Supports publishing separate miss/false-alert rates and linking each level to concrete actions rather than presenting one accuracy number.
quality_rating: High: author-hosted full paper and ScienceDirect article page read; operational evidence, not evidence for ML calibration.
